content: Vaccines have proven to be highly effective in preventing severe cases of COVID-19, a disease with limited treatment options that can result in long-term disability or death. Achieving widespread vaccination against COVID-19 is critical, as it not only protects individuals who are unable to receive the vaccine but also reduces the likelihood of new, vaccine-resistant mutations of SARS-CoV-2 emerging. Although various COVID-19 vaccines are now widely accessible in many regions, vaccine hesitancy remains a significant barrier to achieving nationwide vaccination coverage in numerous countries, posing a serious threat to public health. This scoping review aimed to identify and map interventions designed to increase COVID-19 vaccine uptake and reduce vaccine hesitancy. The objective was to explore the existing body of research on strategies to enhance vaccine acceptance across different populations, categorize these interventions, and assess their effectiveness. The review also sought to identify the populations targeted by these interventions and the types of strategies employed. To gather relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register, Web of Science, WHO COVID-19 Global Literature on Coronavirus Disease, PsycINFO, and CINAHL, up to October 11, 2021. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized studies of interventions (NRSIs), observational studies, and case studies with more than 100 participants. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses were also included. However, studies focusing on vaccine hesitancy for diseases other than COVID-19 were excluded. The data were analyzed using a pre-specified protocol uploaded to the Open Science Framework. An interactive scoping map was created to visualize the findings, categorizing interventions into six main types: communication interventions, policy interventions, educational interventions, financial and non-financial incentives, interventions to improve access, and multidimensional interventions. The outcomes of the studies, the countries in which they were conducted, the populations targeted, and whether the study design was randomized or non-randomized were also mapped. A total of 96 studies were included in the review, comprising 61 studies with published results and 35 ongoing studies. Among the published studies, 46 were RCTs, and 15 were NRSIs. The interventions examined were diverse, with communication strategies being the most commonly tested approach to increase vaccine uptake. Most studies measured willingness to get vaccinated as the primary outcome. The majority of these studies were conducted in high-income, English-speaking countries, and many utilized digital interventions in online settings. The populations targeted were varied, including healthcare workers, ethnic minorities in the United States, students, military personnel, at-risk patients, and the general public. Of the 35 ongoing studies, 29 are RCTs, and six are NRSIs. Educational and communication interventions were the most frequently employed strategies in these studies. Unlike the published studies, most ongoing research is not being conducted online. The populations addressed in these studies include minority groups in the United States, healthcare workers, and students. Eleven of the ongoing studies are expected to be completed in 2022. The authors concluded that this scoping review successfully identified and mapped a wide range of interventions aimed at increasing COVID-19 vaccine uptake and reducing vaccine hesitancy. The findings highlight that this is an active area of research, with 61 published studies and 35 ongoing studies. The review provides a comprehensive overview of existing interventions and serves as a foundation for future systematic reviews to evaluate the effectiveness of these strategies. However, significant research gaps were identified, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, as well as in studies focusing on policy interventions, improved vaccine access, and interventions targeting children and adolescents. As COVID-19 vaccines become more widely available, it is essential to address these gaps to ensure equitable and effective vaccination efforts globally.
